description: While out hunting I was able to find and identify a small specimen of American beech (Fagus grandiflora it.) This individual was around 7 feet tall and just over an inch in diameter. description:
Out for a rural drive in the countryside, we encountered an area with an unusual concentration of beautiful yellow-brown leaves still on trees, in November when most trees such as the Maples were already denuded. Oaks drop their leaves here later than others, but these were clearly not Oak leaves, in shape or colour. 

I stopped to get a good look at a leaf. It seemed such an ordinary nondescript shape that I lost hope of identifying it - it must be one of those innumerable trees that all look the same to me. Elms and Poplars and so on are just names to me that I know nothing about. 

So I showed a photo to iNaturalist, and lo and behold, it was suggested that these were Beech leaves. Oh my. Sure enough, I looked around and found myself surrounded by the distinctive smooth trunks of Beech Trees. In fact, I have never found myself in such a beautiful grove of Beech Trees anywhere. There were magnificent specimens of all sizes as far as one could see - and what's more, not a single one was marred by immature juvenile graffiti. 

The narrow gravel road on the steep slopes along Whetstone Run was a little scary because there was so little room to pass if another car were to come along, it would be hard to find a place to pull over even if one wanted to go for a walk, but its remoteness surely contributed to the dramatic beauty of the woodland. I'd certainly like to return (though I'm not equipped for Winter wilderness survival) to see this magical forest in its different seasons. 

Where I stopped to admire the trees was just into West Virginia, above Wheeling Creek, at an elevation of around 320 meters (1050 feet).

description: American beech is common in the woods of Lowndes County (MS), and apparently enjoyed by sapsuckers (note the rows of holes in the trunk). The marcescent leaves -- browning in the fall, but remaining on the trees over winter -- make beeches very visible in mostly bare December woods. Leaf retention is a trait shared with oaks, which are relatives. Most of the trees I spotted were young ones, perhaps because most of the local woods are cut-over secondary forest, or perhaps because larger, more mature trees are less prone to hold their leaves or more exposed to defoliating winds. Long, slender, spear-point like beech buds are also distinctive among the local deciduous trees. Only *Amelanchier* buds are similar, and they are neither as long nor as slender.
